summary: Starts the deprecation of triple-DES (3DES) and RC4 encryption types in Kerberos because their cryptographic strength is weakening. RFC 4757 was moved to Historic, and RFC 3961 was updated to note that the triple-DES types are deprecated. It is Best Current Practice guidance for implementers and administrators.

eli5.summary: Two old locks keep getting easier to pick. This tells everyone who uses Kerberos to stop buying them and switch to stronger ones.

questions: why deprecate 3des and rc4 in kerberos
what encryption does kerberos use now
subtitle: Moving Kerberos away from weakening encryption methods for authentication security.

tldr.problem: Triple-DES and RC4 encryption types, long used for Kerberos authentication, have steadily weakening cryptographic strength. RC4 has statistical biases and relies on weak password hashing; 3DES suffers from weak key derivation and a small block size that allows collision attacks.
tldr.mechanism: This document moves RFC 4757 (RC4 specification) to Historic status and updates RFCs 3961 and 4120 to officially deprecate these encryption types, recommending that implementations and deployments stop using them in favor of stronger AES encryption.
tldr.outcome: AES has been available in Kerberos implementations and Windows since 2004-2008, providing a secure alternative. Systems can now migrate away from these weakened methods, though some legacy systems may face temporary interoperability constraints during transition.

today: RFC 8429 is Best Current Practice and remains active. It updated RFC 3961 and RFC 4120 to formally deprecate 3DES and RC4 in Kerberos. Administrators and implementers should use AES exclusively for new deployments and migrate existing systems away from these weakened encryption types.

sections.title: The Problem with Old Encryption
sections.content:
Kerberos is a network authentication system that uses encryption to protect credentials and tickets. For decades, it relied on Triple-DES (3DES) and RC4 as encryption types—the algorithms that scramble sensitive data. Both have served well, but cryptographic research has steadily weakened them, and computing power has grown faster than their security margins.

This document is a best current practice guideline telling Kerberos administrators and implementers to stop using these two encryption types. The specific algorithms affected are 3DES variants with code numbers 5, 7, and 16, and RC4-HMAC (code 23).
sections.eli5: Two old ways of scrambling passwords in Kerberos are not safe anymore. This tells everyone to stop using them.

sections.title: Why These Ciphers Are Weak
sections.content:
Both 3DES and RC4 have fundamental vulnerabilities that make them unsuitable for continued use. These are not newly discovered flaws, but rather long-understood weaknesses that have become more practical to exploit as computing power has grown. The document provides specific technical reasons for each cipher.

Beyond raw cryptographic strength, Kerberos's use of these ciphers compounds the problems. The way Kerberos derives encryption keys from passwords is particularly weak for both RC4 and 3DES, using old, non-standard methods that do not incorporate modern best practices like PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2).
sections.eli5: Both old locks have weak points. Even worse, the way Kerberos used them made the weak points worse.

sections.title: RC4: Multiple Failure Points
sections.content:
RC4 is a stream cipher known to have statistical biases in its output keystream—certain bits are more predictable than others. These biases have led to practical attacks on RC4 when used in TLS. In Kerberos, the biases extend well past the initial confounder (a random prefix that partially mitigates the issue), leaving potential attack surface.

More critically, RC4's password-hashing function is fundamentally flawed. It uses a single iteration of the old MD4 hash with no salt—no unique value tied to each user or realm. This allows attackers to precompute rainbow tables: pre-calculated hash tables of common passwords that work across all Kerberos realms simultaneously. An attacker with such a table can compromise any user whose password is weak.

A third vulnerability stems from legacy compatibility. RC4's unsalted MD4 hash was deliberately designed to match the NT LAN Manager (NTLM) protocol, allowing old systems to migrate from NTLM to Kerberos in place. Today, many application servers still hold NTLM password hashes from users, inadvertently giving them the Kerberos keys for those users—a cross-protocol leakage of sensitive material.
sections.eli5: RC4 has three big problems: its scrambling method has predictable patterns, its password hashing is too simple (no salt), and it was designed to match an even older broken system.

sections.title: 3DES: Slow and Vulnerable
sections.content:
Triple-DES inherits the fundamental weaknesses of single-DES, just with more key material. The password-hashing function used for 3DES (specifically the des3-cbc-sha1-kd type) is an ad hoc n-fold construction that, while better than RC4's approach, does not use the computationally demanding PBKDF2 algorithm. It is vulnerable to brute-force dictionary attacks on common passwords.

More problematic is 3DES's 64-bit block size. Block ciphers divide plaintext into fixed chunks and encrypt each chunk. With 3DES, an attacker collecting roughly 2^32 blocks (256 GB) of ciphertext encrypted with the same key can find a collision via the birthday attack—two different plaintext blocks that encrypt to the same ciphertext. While this does not necessarily leak the key itself, it reveals plaintext, a significant weakness.

Finally, 3DES is slow. Its triple-encryption design makes it computationally expensive compared to modern ciphers like AES, which now benefit from hardware acceleration on modern CPUs. Unlike RC4, which some systems might rely on for compatibility, no Kerberos deployment prefers 3DES over AES for performance.
sections.eli5: 3DES is slow, uses weak password hashing, and its small block size lets attackers spot repeated messages with enough ciphertext.

sections.title: The Interoperability Reality
sections.content:
A common concern with any deprecation is backward compatibility. Some older systems still run RC4 exclusively: Windows XP and Windows Server 2003 support only single-DES and RC4 (single-DES was already deprecated in RFC 6649). Similarly, some cross-realm Kerberos keys were established when only RC4 was available.

However, modern Kerberos implementations have provided secure alternatives for years. AES has been available since 2004 in MIT Kerberos 1.3.2, since 2005 in Heimdal 0.7, and since Windows Vista and Server 2008 in Microsoft Windows (2007–2008). Over 12 years of deployment makes it very likely that the vast majority of Kerberos deployments already support AES. For the few systems running decade-old unsupported software, administrators will need to plan migration strategies or run isolated compatibility shims, but these are rare edge cases.
sections.eli5: Some very old computers only know RC4, but modern computers have used stronger AES since the mid-2000s. Most systems can switch now.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
This document formally updates the Kerberos specification RFCs to remove recommendations for 3DES and RC4. It directs implementers and operators to stop using the four deprecated encryption types (3DES variants 5, 7, 16 and RC4-HMAC 23), and to stop implementing related checksum types (RSA-MD5, RSA-MD5-DES3, and two HMAC variants tied to 3DES).

For existing Kerberos systems, this is a planning document: organizations should inventory their deployments, confirm AES support, and schedule migration. For new deployments, the decision is straightforward: AES is the only acceptable choice.
sections.eli5: Stop using RC4 and 3DES in Kerberos. Use AES instead. If you have old systems, plan how to switch them.
